cf.title: Add table COMMENTS in CREATE TABLE LIKE

input.subject: COMMENTS are not being copied in CREATE TABLE LIKE

verdict_reasoning: The decisive objection is demand-1: the thread shows no user or workflow that needs the table comment copied, and Tom Lane (message #34) and Tomas Vondra (message #33) asked for one. demand-2 adds that every `including all` user gets the new comment and has no exact spelling for the old result. Both are fixable and fit "not now, show demand". Design objections at level 2 were not evaluated.

brief.title: Copy the table comment in create table like including comments
brief.problem: Create table (like ... including comments), and so including all, copies comments on columns, constraints, indexes and extended statistics, but not the comment on the source table itself. The author found this while reviewing another patch and first called it a bug. Reviewers noted the documentation lists only those objects, so the change is a feature, and no user has asked for it.
brief.proposed_design: v5 copies the source relation's comment to the new table under including comments when the command has exactly one like clause. With several like clauses, no table comment is copied, but comments on columns and other objects still are. v4 concatenated multiple table comments with newlines; v5 drops that.
user_visible_surface: Changed behaviour of `including comments` in `create table ... (like ...)`: the source relation's own comment is copied.
Changed behaviour of `including all`, which now also copies the table comment.
Applies to `create foreign table ... (like ...)` too; v4 fixed an error in v3 for foreign table targets.
A composite type used as a like source passes its type comment to the new table, as v4 regression tests show.
author_claims: Copying makes including comments cover every comment on the objects that like copies.
No single source comment describes a table built from several sources, so v5 skips that case.
Users who do not want the table comment can write `including all excluding comments`.
A reviewer reported tests passed and saw no performance change, including a case with hundreds of source tables.
brief.thread_state: Tom Lane and Tomas Vondra question the lack of a real use case, and Tom would wait for field requests; the author then posted v5 without multi-table support and agreed the use case is the root issue. No one has replied to v5, and the patch has moved through four CommitFests.
unclear: The material shows no user request or concrete workflow that needs the table comment copied.
Nobody in the thread says whether Tom Lane's objection to the whole feature still holds after v5.
The patch does not say whether a type comment should be copied when the like source is a composite type; the author leaned toward removing it.
The thread does not settle whether including all should change for existing scripts, which Hüseyin Demir raised.

prior_attempts.title: create table like: ACCESS METHOD
prior_attempts.who_objected: Peter Eisentraut, Michael Paquier, Vik Fearing
prior_attempts.quote: Whereas the access method is a table property. So I don't think this syntax is the right approach for this feature.
prior_attempts.reason: LIKE expands to column definitions, but the access method is a table property, so two LIKE clauses with different access methods can conflict. Its interaction with USING is also undefined. The patch overwrote any AM given in USING, and Michael Paquier asked for a clear definition of these corner cases. Peter Eisentraut argued that this syntax is the wrong approach and suggested something like USING (LIKE t1).
prior_attempts.what_is_different: It copies the table comment and not the access method, so there is no clash with USING. v5 avoids the multi-LIKE conflict by copying no table comment when there are several LIKE clauses.

prior_attempts.title: Proposal to have INCLUDE/EXCLUDE options for altering option values
prior_attempts.quote: Also, I'm not convinced that this problem would arise often enough in practice that it's worth adding a feature to address it.
prior_attempts.reason: Robert Haas and Euler Taveira doubted the use case was common enough to justify new syntax, since a user can read the option value, edit the list and SET it again. They also noted that most options are not lists and that list options need not be comma-separated. Euler Taveira added that the actions are not idempotent and that REMOVE is confusing next to DROP. The author agreed and withdrew the patch.
prior_attempts.what_is_different: It is a different feature that added new syntax for foreign server options. Only the doubt about real-world need is shared.

objections.title: No field request or workflow shows anyone needs the table comment copied
objections.failure_scenario: A committer commits v5 to close a gap noticed during patch review. Later a real user turns up whose workflow needs different semantics, for example first-wins with several LIKE clauses or no copying of type comments. The project then has to change shipped behaviour of including comments a second time.
objections.argument: The patch started because the feature was missing (message #1), and no user report has appeared since. Tomas Vondra could not build a meaningful example (message #33), and Tom Lane would wait for field requests before choosing semantics (message #34). The author agreed that the missing use case is the root issue (messages #36, #37). Dropping multi-table support narrows the patch but does not add a user. The workaround, a comment on table statement after create table, costs one line, as in [P9].
objections.author_must_show: Which users or tools today run create table like and then copy the table comment by hand, and what do they expect when several like clauses are used?

precedents.title: Proposal to have INCLUDE/EXCLUDE options for altering option values

critic.reasoning: The thread shows no user request. Tom Lane (#34) and Tomas Vondra (#33) ask for one, and the author agrees in #36 and #37. [P9] concerned new syntax, so it is only weak support.

objections.title: Changing including all affects existing scripts for an unproven gain
objections.failure_scenario: A deployment script clones a template table commented 'template, do not use directly' with including all. After an upgrade, every derived table carries that comment. Users and catalog-browsing tools read it as a description of the new table. The script owner finds out only when someone asks why production tables are marked as templates.
objections.argument: Hüseyin Demir raised this in messages #11 and #13. The author's answer, including all excluding comments (message #14), also drops column, constraint and index comments, so the old result has no exact spelling. The script must instead add comment on table ... is null. Every including all user pays this cost, and the material names no user who gains.
objections.author_must_show: What evidence shows that more including all users want the table comment copied than users who would now have to remove it?

critic.reasoning: Message #14 answers that any LIKE extension changes `including all`, but this patch also changes the existing `including comments` option, and `excluding comments` drops the column comments too. The cost is one extra statement, so fixable is the right severity.

other_surviving.title: Per-clause option whose effect depends on how many LIKE clauses exist
other_surviving.failure_scenario: A user writes `like t1 including comments` and gets t1's table comment. Later they add `like audit_cols excluding all` to append audit columns, and the table comment disappears without notice. Nothing in that clause asked for this.
other_surviving.argument: `including comments` is an option of one LIKE clause, but the table comment is a property of the whole new table. Message #36 says v5 counts LIKE clauses and skips the table comment when the count is not 1, so an `excluding` clause changes the result of an `including` clause. [P1] stalled on the same mismatch: a table-level property was attached to a per-clause option, and it had no defined meaning across several clauses. The documentation hunk states the rule but does not explain why the count is the right test.
other_surviving.author_must_show: Why should a clause that excludes comments stop another clause from copying its table comment, and should the rule count only clauses with including comments?

critic.reasoning: Message #36 and the v5 documentation hunk both make the rule a count of LIKE clauses, so a clause with `excluding all` removes the table comment. [P1] applies, because it too attached a table-level property to a per-clause option.

other_surviving.not_ranked_reason: level 2 is above the failing level 1b: not evaluated (base-up stop rule)

other_surviving.title: Type and view comments become table comments without a decision
other_surviving.failure_scenario: A user runs `create table t (like mytype including comments)` on a composite type whose comment describes the type, for example 'return type of f()'. The new table gets that text as its table comment. They notice only when reading `\dt+` or generated schema docs.
other_surviving.argument: Message #29 shows the v4 tests copy a composite type's comment into pg_class for the new table. The author leaned toward removing this, but no one replied, and the v5 documentation hunk speaks only of the source relation's comment. A type comment and a table comment describe different kinds of object. Once this ships, removing it later is itself a behaviour change.
other_surviving.author_must_show: Which source kinds (table, view, foreign table, composite type) pass their comment to the new table in v5, and why is each one right?

critic.reasoning: Message #29 asks whether a composite type's comment should be copied, and nobody answered. The v5 commit message and documentation say only "source relation", so the material does not settle which source kinds pass their comment on.

other_surviving.not_ranked_reason: level 2 is above the failing level 1b: not evaluated (base-up stop rule)

refuted.title: No field request shown, and v5 does not answer the request for one
refuted.failure_scenario: The project commits a behaviour change to including comments and including all with no known user. When a user later reports a workflow that needs a different rule, such as the multi-LIKE case, the single-LIKE rule is already released and has to stay compatible.
refuted.argument: In message #34 Tom Lane would rather pass until field requests arrive, because any behaviour chosen might be wrong for real usage. Tomas Vondra (message #33) says the patch came from "it's missing", not from a need. In message #36 the author calls the missing use case the root issue and drops multi-LIKE support, but no use case is added. [P9] was withdrawn on a similar doubt that the problem arises often enough.
refuted.author_must_show: Which user or workflow today needs the source table comment copied by create table like, and what does that user do now instead?

precedents.title: Proposal to have INCLUDE/EXCLUDE options for altering option values

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of demand-1, which makes the same point from messages #33, #34 and #36 and also names the existing one-statement alternative.

refuted.title: Table comment disappears when a second like clause is added
refuted.failure_scenario: A deployment script runs create table t (like tmpl including all) and gets the comment of tmpl. Later someone adds like audit_cols including all to the same command. The comment of t is then silently lost, and nobody notices until someone reads the catalog or the docs.
refuted.argument: In [P1] a table-level property copied through LIKE was rejected because LIKE expands to column definitions, while the property belongs to the table, and several LIKE clauses can conflict. v5 avoids the conflict by copying nothing when there are several LIKE clauses. Because of that, the result of one LIKE clause now depends on whether another LIKE clause is present, and Postgres raises no notice. No one has commented on v5 since it was posted in message #36.
refuted.author_must_show: Why is a silent drop on multiple LIKE clauses better than an error or a separate table-level option, given that LIKE is otherwise column-oriented?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of standards-compat-2, which describes the same silent loss and adds that a clause with `excluding all` also triggers it.

refuted.title: No way to keep the old result except dropping all comments
refuted.failure_scenario: A provisioning script runs `create table stage_x (like template include all)` against a template commented 'template, do not use directly'. After upgrade, every new staging table carries that comment and documentation tools pick it up. The only spelling that removes it, `excluding comments`, also drops the column, constraint and index comments the script relied on.
refuted.argument: Hüseyin Demir raised this change to `including all` in messages #11 and #13 and noted the old behaviour can no longer be expressed. The answer in message #14, `including all excluding comments`, does not give the old result, because it also removes the per-column comments. Nobody replied after that, and v5 does not add a separate switch. A committer would likely ask for an opt-in or opt-out that targets only the table comment.
refuted.author_must_show: How does a user on the new release get exactly the pre-upgrade result, with column and index comments copied and no table comment?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of demand-2. Its claim that the old result cannot be expressed is too strong, because `comment on table ... is null` after the command restores it, as demand-2 says.

refuted.title: Single-LIKE rule makes the table comment depend on clause count
refuted.failure_scenario: A user runs `create table t2 (like t1 including all)` and gets t1's comment. Later they add `like audit_cols including all` to the same command to pick up shared columns. The table comment is then dropped with no notice, and they find out only when someone reads the catalog.
refuted.argument: LIKE mostly copies column-level objects. A table comment is a property of the whole relation, so several LIKE clauses can conflict, and v5 settles this by counting clauses (message #36). [P1] was returned for this same reason when LIKE tried to copy the access method. Every later table-level INCLUDING option would need its own conflict rule, and nothing reports when the rules disagree.
refuted.author_must_show: Why should adding a second LIKE clause drop the table comment silently, and what common rule would later table-level INCLUDING options follow?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of standards-compat-2. Its extra point about later table-level INCLUDING options has no concrete failure scenario in the material.

refuted.title: Release fixes multi-LIKE behaviour before any use case exists
refuted.failure_scenario: v5 ships with "multiple LIKE copies no table comment" and scripts come to rely on it. A field request later asks for first-wins or concatenation. Changing the rule then alters the output of `including all` a second time for existing scripts.
refuted.argument: In message #34 Tom Lane asks to wait for field requests because any rule chosen now might be wrong for real usage. v5 removes the hardest case, but it still picks one rule for that case without such evidence. The thread shows no user request (messages #33, #37), and nobody has replied to v5 to say Tom's concern is resolved. This fits "not now, show demand" better than a rejection on the merits.
refuted.author_must_show: Which users or workflows need the table comment copied, and does what they need agree with the v5 rule for multiple LIKE clauses?

critic.reasoning: With several LIKE clauses, v5 copies no table comment, which is what Postgres does today, so v5 fixes no new rule for that case. The remaining demand point is covered by demand-1.

refuted.title: One comment on table statement already does what v5 automates
refuted.failure_scenario: A script that runs `create table t2 (like t1 including all)` from a template whose comment says "template, do not use directly" now gives every derived table that comment. The owner notices later in `\dt+` or in pg_dump output. A user who did want the comment gained one statement fewer.
refuted.argument: After the `create table`, `comment on table t2 is ...` sets the comment. Copying it from the source takes one psql line, `select format('comment on table %I is %L', 't2', obj_description('t1'::regclass, 'pg_class')) \gexec`, or a `do` block with `execute`. So the existing way can do the job with modest effort, as message #6 notes. The cost falls on existing `including all` users (messages #11 and #13), and the material shows no user who asked for this (messages #33 and #34).
refuted.author_must_show: Which users today copy table comments after create table like, and why is one comment on table statement not enough for them?

precedents.title: Proposal to have INCLUDE/EXCLUDE options for altering option values

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of demand-1, which already names the `comment on table` alternative. The cost to existing `including all` users is covered by demand-2.

touch_points.label: SQL-standard conflict or non-standard syntax
touch_points.reason: The patch changes what `including comments` and `including all` mean in `create table ... (like ...)`.

touch_points.label: backpatchability
touch_points.reason: Message #2 asked for a backpatch, but message #3 classes the change as an improvement, so it is for the next major version only.

touch_points.label: maintenance burden ("who maintains this in 10 years")
touch_points.reason: The single-LIKE rule and the set of source kinds that pass a comment become released behaviour to keep compatible.

touch_points.label: doesn't fit what Postgres is about (extension / external tool / already solved)
touch_points.reason: A `comment on table` statement after `create table` already gives the same result in one line.

questions: Which users or tools today run `create table ... (like ...)` and then copy the table comment by hand, and what do they expect with several LIKE clauses?
What evidence shows that more `including all` users want the table comment copied than users who would now have to remove it?
How does a user on the new release copy column, constraint and index comments but no table comment in one command?
Why should a second LIKE clause with `excluding all` stop the first clause from copying its table comment?
Which source kinds (table, view, foreign table, composite type) pass their comment to the new table in v5, and why is each one right?

committability.owner_note: Tom Lane and Tomas Vondra took part (messages #33, #34), but both questioned the need and neither has replied to v5. The owner would be someone who knows the LIKE expansion code in parse_utilcmd.c.
committability.liability: The owner signs for a permanent behaviour change of `including comments` and `including all`, for the single-LIKE rule, and for which source kinds pass their comment. The code itself is small.
committability.author_follow_up: The author posted five versions over about nine months, dropped multi-table support after feedback, and moved the entry between CommitFests.

not_now.evidence_that_would_change_it: A field report, a pgsql-general or pgsql-bugs thread, or a named tool that copies table comments after `create table ... (like ...)`, with the behaviour it expects for several LIKE clauses and for composite type sources. An argument that the change to `including all` hurts fewer users than it helps would also count.

priority.reason: The patch is about 15 KiB in the parser, docs and regression tests, so it is cheap to review and carry. The thread names no user, and two committers asked to wait for a field request, so more review now does not move it forward.

provisional_note: The code was not read, so the exact v5 behaviour for view, foreign table and composite type sources is unverified, as is how v5 counts LIKE clauses. The level 2 objections standards-compat-2 and standards-compat-3 survived but were not evaluated because level 1b fails first.
disclosure: Prepared by an AI harness; treat as a devil's advocate, not a verdict.

precedents_retrieved.title: create table like: ACCESS METHOD
precedents_retrieved.objectors: Peter Eisentraut, Michael Paquier, Vik Fearing
precedents_retrieved.summary: Add an ACCESS METHOD option to CREATE TABLE ... LIKE, so that INCLUDING ACCESS METHOD (and INCLUDING ALL) copies the source table's table access method to the new table. Partitioned tables would silently ignore the option.
precedents_retrieved.objection: LIKE expands to column definitions, but the access method is a table property, so two LIKE clauses with different access methods can conflict. Its interaction with USING is also undefined. The patch overwrote any AM given in USING, and Michael Paquier asked for a clear definition of these corner cases. Peter Eisentraut argued that this syntax is the wrong approach and suggested something like USING (LIKE t1).
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: Whereas the access method is a table property.  So I don't think this syntax is the right approach for this feature.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert "Distinguish printf-like functions that support %m from those that don't."
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert "Distinguish printf-like functions that support %m from those that don't."
Reverted commit(s): Distinguish printf-like functions that support %m from those that don't.
precedents_retrieved.objection:
This reverts commit 3a60c8ff892a8242b907f44702bfd9f1ff877d45.  Buildfarm
results show that that caused a whole bunch of new warnings on platforms
where gcc believes the local printf to be non-POSIX-compliant.  This
problem outweighs the hypothetical-anyway possibility of getting warnings
for misuse of %m.  We could use gnu_printf archetype when we've substituted
src/port/snprintf.c, but that brings us right back to the problem of not
getting warnings for %m.

A possible answer is to attack it in the other direction by insisting
that %m support be included in printf's feature set, but that will take
more investigation.  In the meantime, revert the previous change, and
update the comment for PGAC_C_PRINTF_ARCHETYPE to more fully explain
what's going on.

This commit reverts 1adf16b8fb, 87c21bb941, and subsequent fixes and

842c9b2705, fcf80c5d5f, 96c7381c4c, f4fc7cb54b, 60ae37a8bc, 259c96fa8f,

precedents_retrieved.title: Create shorthand for including all extra tests
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds an 'all' value for PG_TEST_EXTRA, checked through a new check_extra_tests_enabled() function in Test/Utils.pm, so a full run includes every extra test suite. After feedback it replaced 'all' with a 'needs-private-lo' category that enables the kerberos, ldap, load_balance and ssl tests.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane objected that the extra tests are excluded by default because they are security hazards, so each should be reviewed before it is enabled. Peter Eisentraut said 'needs-private-lo' is not the only condition, since kerberos and ldap need extra software and load_balance may need edits to the hosts file. He also preferred each test deciding on its own over a central mapping, and saw no sensible grouping for six values. The author agreed to revisit the idea if more PG_TEST_EXTRA options appear.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
So someone would still need to familiarize themselves with these tests
individually before setting a global option like this.

precedents_retrieved.title: Add --include-table-data-where option to pg_dump, to export only a subset of table data
precedents_retrieved.summary: Add a pg_dump option (initially --include-table-data-where=table:filter_clause, later discussed as --where) that applies a user-supplied WHERE clause to the data dump of tables matching a pattern, so that only a subset of rows is exported. The option could be given multiple times, and each filter applied to every table matching its pattern.
precedents_retrieved.objection: It was returned with feedback because the patch had merge conflicts and was not rebased after a reviewer asked for it; the author posted a rebased patch only after the entry had been closed. Reviewers had also raised open design points about the option syntax: the use of a colon to separate table from clause, how colons in table or column names would be parsed, and how the option interacts with --table. One participant also questioned whether the feature was needed, given psql \copy.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: Given this patch has not been updated, I'm marking this as returned with feedback.

precedents_retrieved.title: Remove unused #include's
precedents_retrieved.objectors: Andres Freund, Álvaro Herrera, Tom Lane, Nathan Bossart
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch removes #include lines that clangd, and later include-what-you-use, reported as unused. It started with src/backend/commands and then grew to cover all of src/.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The author withdrew the patch after senior reviewers objected. Several removals broke builds under other platforms or options, and some removed headers were still included through other headers, so the source did not improve. Tom Lane said past bad experiences with automated #include removal make developers wary of work that may need undoing, and Nathan Bossart did not want hundreds of small cleanup commits.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
The currently available tools are probably smarter
than what we were using back then, but they're evidently still not
perfect, and we're leery of having to undo work.

precedents_retrieved.summary:

precedents_retrieved.title: Proposal to have INCLUDE/EXCLUDE options for altering option values
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds two new actions, APPEND and REMOVE, to the OPTIONS clause of ALTER SERVER and similar commands for foreign servers, user mappings and foreign tables. They add values to or remove values from a comma-separated option value without restating the whole list.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Robert Haas and Euler Taveira doubted the use case was common enough to justify new syntax, since a user can read the option value, edit the list and SET it again. They also noted that most options are not lists and that list options need not be comma-separated. Euler Taveira added that the actions are not idempotent and that REMOVE is confusing next to DROP. The author agreed and withdrew the patch.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
Also, I'm not convinced
that this problem would arise often enough in practice that it's worth
adding a feature to address it.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert analyze support for partitioned tables
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert analyze support for partitioned tables
Reverted commit(s): Describe (auto-)analyze behavior for partitioned tables; Set pg_class.reltuples for partitioned tables; Document ANALYZE storage parameters for partitioned tables; autovacuum: handle analyze for partitioned tables; Don't reset relhasindex for partitioned tables on ANALYZE
precedents_retrieved.objection:
This reverts the following commits:
1b5617eb844cd2470a334c1d2eec66cf9b39c41a Describe (auto-)analyze behavior for partitioned tables
0e69f705cc1a3df273b38c9883fb5765991e04fe Set pg_class.reltuples for partitioned tables
41badeaba8beee7648ebe7923a41c04f1f3cb302 Document ANALYZE storage parameters for partitioned tables
0827e8af70f4653ba17ed773f123a60eadd9f9c9 autovacuum: handle analyze for partitioned tables

There are efficiency issues in this code when handling databases with
large numbers of partitions, and it doesn't look like there isn't any
trivial way to handle those.  There are some other issues as well.  It's
now too late in the cycle for nontrivial fixes, so we'll have to let
Postgres 14 users continue to manually deal with ANALYZE their
partitioned tables, and hopefully we can fix the issues for Postgres 15.

I kept [most of] be280cdad298 ("Don't reset relhasindex for partitioned
tables on ANALYZE") because while we added it due to 0827e8af70f4, it is
a good bugfix in its own right, since it affects manual analyze as well
as autovacuum-induced analyze, and there's no reason to revert it.

I retained the addition of relkind 'p' to tables included by
pg_stat_user_tables, because reverting that would require a catversion
bump.
Also, in pg14 only, I keep a struct member that was added to
PgStat_TabStatEntry to avoid breaking compatibility with existing stat
files.

Backpatch to 14.

precedents_retrieved.title: COPY WHERE clause generated/system column reference
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patches make COPY FROM ... WHERE work with generated columns: they expand virtual generated columns in the WHERE clause and compute stored generated columns before the WHERE clause is checked. They also reject system columns other than tableoid in the WHERE clause.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Peter Eisentraut committed a smaller fix that rejects generated columns in COPY FROM WHERE with a clear error, and left tableoid for a separate thread. He then argued that support should not be added, because generated columns belong to the target table while the WHERE clause filters input data. Masahiko Sawada had shown that computing stored generated columns before the WHERE clause runs them before BEFORE INSERT triggers, so the WHERE clause changes the row the trigger sees.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
This seems fundamentally wrong, because generated columns are a
property of the target table, but the COPY WHERE clause is meant to
filter the input data.

precedents_retrieved.title: table inheritance versus column compression and storage settings
precedents_retrieved.summary: Change how MergeAttributes() handles column compression and storage settings under table inheritance, treating them as physical per-table properties. A new child inherits the parent's settings but can override them, attaching a child changes nothing, and conflicting settings from multiple parents require an explicit setting in the child.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The committed patch was reverted after Tom Lane showed that pg_dump and pg_restore of the regression database fail: stchild4 does not restore and stchild5 gets the wrong attstorage. Ashutosh Bapat then found related existing dump bugs and proposed setting defaults when parents conflict. Peter Eisentraut declined to take on that change late in the cycle, citing unexpected pitfalls, missing test coverage and no patch.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
We have already discovered with the previous attempt that
there are unexpected pitfalls and lacking test coverage.  Also, there
isn't even a patch yet.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert "Propagate CTE property flags when copying a CTE list into a rule."

precedents_retrieved.title: Allow logical replication via inheritance root table
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch lets an extension or user mark an existing inheritance child so that logical replication publishes its changes through a chosen parent, reusing the publish_via_partition_root machinery. It adds a publisher-side function that tells the subscriber which tables to COPY during initial sync, and later a publish_via_parent reloption set with ALTER TABLE.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The author paused the entry after finding that the subscriber side could not handle the routed data: when incoming tuples are moved to other tables, a later UPDATE or DELETE checks the root table and does not find the rows. He decided to work on subscriber-side support first. Amit Kapila also said that one extension's needs are not a reason to accept the feature in core.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: Given that, I think I need to pivot and focus on the subscriber side first. That might(?) be a smaller effort anyway, and if we can't make headway there then publisher-side support probably doesn't make sense at all.

Revert "Remove reset of testtablespace from pg_regress on Windows"
Reverted commit(s): Remove reset of testtablespace from pg_regress on Windows; Lower privilege level of programs calling regression_main
precedents_retrieved.objection:
This reverts commit 2b2a070, that moved the reset of path
"testtablespace" used by the regression tests as a path for tablespaces
(via --outputdir) from pg_regress to the MSVC script vcregress.pl, as
this broke the behavior added by ce5d342 to be able to safely run the
regression test suite with an administrative Windows account using a
restricted token.

Note that before 2b2a070, the code doing the reset in pg_regress.c
included a comment telling that we had better move that out to a
different place, leading to the mistake done in 2b2a070.  Fix this
comment, and document instead that we had better never remove this code,
for the sake of not breaking again the behavior we expect on Windows.

Thanks to Thomas Munro and Andrew Dunstan for the discussion.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert to the pre-8.2 method of probing for libm, that is, always include it if it links properly.
precedents_retrieved.summary: Revert to the pre-8.2 method of probing for libm, that is, always include it if it links properly.  It seems too risky to assume that standard functions like pow() are not special-cased by the compiler. Per report from Andreas Lange that build fails on Solaris cc compiler with -fast.  Even though we don't consider that a supported option, I'm worried that similar issues will arise with other compilers.

roaster_notes.note: Messages #10, #31 and #33 report that the 2009 thread adding including comments does not discuss table comments. Message #21 quotes a wish from that thread to clone all comments reasonably possible. [P3] has no recorded reason that applies.
pg_dump round-trip is not affected: the dump records the resulting table and its comment, not the LIKE clause.

The proposal adds no new persistent or cross-node state. The table comment is written to pg_description through the existing COMMENT path, with no catalog, WAL, on-disk, protocol or ABI change, so pg_upgrade, standbys and pg_dump see an ordinary comment.

No security objection to v5. Comments in pg_description are readable by any role, so copying one into a new table owned by the creator exposes nothing new. The concatenation size concern from messages #31 and #35 no longer applies because v5 drops multi-source concatenation, and copying a single existing comment adds no unbounded allocation. Message #33 notes that setting a comment already requires ownership, so the patch opens no new path for an untrusted role to change what the copy produces.
The patch touches only the parser and docs, has no hot-path cost, and adds no external dependency. Maintenance cost is small apart from the design points above.
One objection from this angle. No contrib module or extension covers this, so the existing way is plain SQL plus psql \gexec or a do block.
Two demand objections. The material shows no user request, and the change of including all falls on users who did not ask for it.
